why_how.text: Most crashes at signals come right after a light changes, so the moments around a change are where care matters most.
Many stops are required by law beyond red lights, including for blind pedestrians, crosswalk users, officers and driveways.

scenario.text: Ana approaches a light that has been green since she turned onto the street two blocks back.

reasoning.text: That is a stale green, so she expects a yellow; when it turns yellow and she has room, she stops before the intersection.

result.text: Ana stops safely before the intersection instead of rushing through on the yellow.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a flashing red light only means slow down.

correction.text: A driver must stop at a red light whether the red is steady or flashing.

memory_support.text: Fresh green, take care; stale green, get ready; yellow, stop if you safely can.

prompt.text: A light ahead has been green for a long time, then turns yellow while you still have room to stop. What do you do?

rationale.text: A stale green is about to change, and a yellow after a green means stop unless you are too close to stop safely.

lines.text: Light changes are risky moments.
Some stops are always required.

narration.text: This lesson is about the moments when a driver has to decide whether to go or to stop. Traffic lights come first. Most crashes at traffic signals happen in the first few seconds after the light changes, so the change itself is the danger point, not the long stretch in between. After the lights, we turn to the places where New Jersey requires a full stop: stop signs, red lights, blind pedestrians, people in crosswalks, officers directing traffic, a yield sign with no safe gap, driveways, and bridges about to open. By the end you will know when stopping is a judgment call and when it is the law.

lines.text: Fresh green: crashes cluster right after the change.
Stale green: already green for some time.
Expect a stale green to turn yellow.

narration.text: Two kinds of green light call for two kinds of attention. A fresh green has just changed, and that is exactly when most crashes at signals happen, in the first few seconds after the light changes. So when your light turns green, move off with care rather than launching the moment it switches. A stale green is the opposite case. It is a light that has already been green for some time, which means it is closer to changing. As you approach a stale green, be ready for it to turn yellow and then red. In both cases the lesson is the same: the moment of change is where you stay most alert.

lines.text: Yellow after green: stop before the intersection.
Too close to stop safely: continue.
Already inside when it changes: continue with caution.

narration.text: Here is a trap many drivers fall into. A yellow light is not a signal to speed up and get through before the red. When a yellow light follows a green, the rule is to stop before the intersection. There is one exception: if you are so close that you cannot stop safely, you continue. And if the light changes while you are already in the intersection, you do not stop in the middle of it. You continue through with caution. So the decision depends on where you are when the yellow appears. Room to stop means stop. No safe room, or already inside, means carry on carefully, and never faster.

lines.text: Stop at stop signs and red lights.
Red means stop, steady or flashing.
Stop when an officer orders it.
Stop leaving alleys, driveways or buildings.

narration.text: Now the list of places where a stop is required. A driver must stop at a stop sign, and at a red light whether the red is steady or flashing. A driver must also stop when a traffic officer orders it, and at a yield sign when traffic does not allow a safe merge. A yield sign normally lets you keep rolling, but if there is no safe gap, you stop. Two more stops are easy to forget. You must stop when coming out of an alley, a private driveway or a building, and you must stop at a bridge span that is about to open for boats. Each of these is a full stop, not a slow roll.

lines.text: Blind pedestrian with a white or metallic cane.
Pedestrian with a trained guide dog.
Pedestrians in a crosswalk or at an intersection.
Motorized wheelchairs and mobility devices.

narration.text: Some required stops are about people rather than signs. A driver must stop for a blind pedestrian who is using a white or metallic cane or a trained guide dog. The same rule covers a guide dog instructor who is training a dog. A driver must also stop for a pedestrian in a crosswalk or at an intersection, and for a person using a motorized wheelchair or another mobility-assistance device there. Notice the pattern. A cane or a guide dog tells you the person is blind, and a crosswalk is a place where people are expected to cross. In every one of these cases, the answer is the same: you stop.

lines.text: A long green turns yellow.
You still have room to stop.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you are driving toward a light that has been green ever since you turned onto the street. As you get closer, it turns yellow, and you still have plenty of room to stop smoothly. What should you do? Work it out before reading on. The answer is to stop before the intersection. The light was a stale green, a light that had already been green for some time, so a change to yellow was something to expect. A yellow that follows a green means stop unless you are too close to stop safely. You had room, so you stop. Speeding up to get through before the red is never the rule.

lines.text: Take care on a fresh green.
Yellow: stop if you safely can.
Red, steady or flashing: stop.
Stop for people, officers, driveways and bridges.

narration.text: Let us pull this lesson together. Most crashes at signals come in the first few seconds after a change, so move off a fresh green with care, and treat a stale green as one that is about to turn. When yellow follows green, stop before the intersection unless you are too close to stop safely, and continue with caution if you are already inside. Stop at every stop sign and every red light, steady or flashing. Stop for blind pedestrians, crosswalk pedestrians and wheelchair users, for an officer's order, at a yield sign with no safe merge, when leaving a driveway, and at a bridge about to open.

why_how.text: A fast train needs over a mile to stop, so every crossing rule puts the burden on the driver.
Crossing warnings tell you to stop well back and to wait until every warning has ended.

scenario.text: Ben drives behind a school bus toward a railroad crossing where no train is signaled.

reasoning.text: School buses must always stop at railroad crossings, so Ben expects the stop and leaves room behind the bus.

result.text: The bus stops, Ben stops behind it, and he crosses later only when there is room to get fully across.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you may stop on the tracks if traffic ahead backs up.

correction.text: Never stop on railroad tracks; make sure there is room to get fully across before you start.

memory_support.text: Fifteen feet back, gates up, bells quiet, then go.

prompt.text: Gates are lowering and bells are ringing at a crossing ahead. Where do you stop, and when may you cross?

answer.text: Stop at least fifteen feet from the crossing, and cross only after the gates are up and the bells and red lights have stopped.

rationale.text: Active warnings mean a fifteen-foot stop, and crossing waits until the gates, bells and red lights have all finished.

lines.text: Trains cannot stop quickly.
Know the warnings and the distances.

narration.text: Railroad crossings are one of the few places where the other vehicle simply cannot stop for you. Most trains moving at sixty miles per hour or more need over a mile to stop, so the whole job of avoiding a crash falls on the driver. In this lesson you will learn what crossing warnings look like, how far back to stop when they are active, when it is safe to cross again, which vehicles always stop at crossings even with no train in sight, and the most important rule of all: never stop on the tracks. Keep that mile in mind, because it explains every rule that follows.

lines.text: Signs, pavement markings, lights, gates, bells, flags.
Active warnings: stop at least fifteen feet back.

narration.text: Crossing warnings come in several forms. You may see advance-warning signs and pavement markings as you approach, and at the crossing itself there may be flashing red lights, gates with or without flashing lights, ringing bells, or a person giving flag signals. When the warnings are active, meaning flashing red lights, ringing bells, gates that are lowering or already down, or flag signals, you must stop at least fifteen feet from the crossing. Notice that any one of those warnings is enough to require the stop; you do not need to see a train first. Fifteen feet is the number for a crossing, so keep it apart from the larger distances used for school buses.

title.text: When to cross, who always stops

lines.text: Cross only when the gates are up.
Bells stopped, red lights stopped flashing.
Buses and hazardous loads always stop.

narration.text: After you stop, the next question is when you may go. Do not cross the tracks until the gates are all the way up, the bells have stopped ringing and the red lights have stopped flashing. All three conditions matter, so a gate that is only starting to rise is not permission. There is also a group of vehicles that stop at every railroad crossing, signal or not. School buses, other buses and vehicles carrying hazardous materials must always stop at railroad crossings. If you are driving behind one of them, be ready to stop as well, even when no train is signaled. Their stop is routine, so it should never surprise you.

title.text: Never race, never stop on tracks

lines.text: Fast trains need over a mile to stop.
Never stop on the tracks.
Warnings start while on the tracks: keep going.

narration.text: Two mistakes cause the worst crossing crashes. The first is racing a train. Most trains moving at sixty miles per hour or more need over a mile to stop, so a driver who tries to get ahead of a train is betting on a stop that cannot happen. Never race a train. The second mistake is stopping on the tracks. Before you start across, make sure there is room on the other side for your whole vehicle to get fully across. If traffic is backed up, wait behind the crossing. And if the warning devices start while you are already on the tracks, do not stop and do not back up. Keep going to the other side.

lines.text: Gates lowering, bells ringing.
Where do you stop, and when do you go?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you are approaching a railroad crossing when the gates begin to lower and the bells start ringing. Where should you stop, and what has to happen before you may cross? Work it out before reading on. You stop at least fifteen feet from the crossing, because active warnings like lowering gates and ringing bells call for that distance. Then you stay stopped until the gates are up, the bells have stopped ringing and the red lights have stopped flashing. A train passing, or a gate that is only beginning to rise, is not enough. All of the warnings must be over before you go.

lines.text: Stop fifteen feet back from active warnings.
Gates up, bells and lights stopped.
Expect buses to stop; never stop on tracks.

narration.text: Here is the railroad lesson in one pass. Warnings can include signs, pavement markings, flashing red lights, gates, bells and flag signals. When they are active, stop at least fifteen feet from the crossing, and cross only after the gates are up, the bells have stopped and the red lights have stopped flashing. Most trains at sixty miles per hour or more need over a mile to stop, so never race one. School buses, buses and hazardous-material vehicles always stop at crossings, so be ready to stop behind them. Never stop on the tracks, and if the warnings start while you are on them, keep going across.

why_how.text: School bus lights tell you when to stop, but they could be broken, so the children are the real signal.
The rule depends on the road: a full stop on most roads, a slow pass across a median or at a school front.

scenario.text: Kim is on a dual-lane highway when she sees a stopped school bus on the other side of a raised median.

reasoning.text: Because a raised median separates her from the bus, the full stop does not apply; she slows to ten miles per hour instead.

result.text: Kim passes at ten miles per hour and keeps watching for children near the road.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a raised median lets you pass a stopped school bus at normal speed.

correction.text: Across a safety island or raised median on a dual-lane highway, you must still slow to ten miles per hour.

memory_support.text: Twenty-five feet to stop, ten to creep, fifteen for ice cream.

prompt.text: On a two-lane road, a school bus ahead stops with red lights flashing. How far back do you stop, and when do you go?

answer.text: Stop at least twenty-five feet away, and move on only once its signals are off.

rationale.text: A two-lane road calls for the twenty-five-foot stop, and even after the signals go off you still watch for children.

lines.text: School buses mean children nearby.
Distances and speeds depend on the road.

narration.text: This lesson is about vehicles that draw children into the road: school buses and ice cream or frozen dessert trucks. A driver must stop when a school bus is picking up or dropping off children or has its red lights flashing. From there the details change with the road. On some roads you stop at a set distance. Across a median you slow down instead. In front of a school you may pass slowly. A dessert truck has its own speed limit and its own exception. The numbers are close together, so we will take them one at a time, and then put them side by side so they stop blurring together.

lines.text: Stop for loading or unloading children.
Stop for flashing red lights.
Bus lights could be broken.

narration.text: Start with when a school bus requires a stop. A driver must stop when a school bus is picking up or dropping off children, or when it has its red lights flashing. School buses normally warn you first. They turn on yellow or amber lights before stopping, and red lights once they have stopped. But the handbook warns that drivers behind a bus should not rely on those lights, because they could be broken. That is why the rule names both conditions. If you see children getting on or off, you stop, whether or not any light is working. The children, not the bulbs, are the signal that matters most.

lines.text: Two-lane road: stop at least twenty-five feet away.
Lines-only multi-lane highway: same rule.
Private road: same rule.
Move on only when signals are off.

narration.text: When a school bus has its red lights flashing, how far back do you stop? At least twenty-five feet away. That distance applies on a two-lane road, on a multi-lane highway whose lanes are separated only by painted lines, and on a privately maintained road. Painted lines do not count as a median. Once you have stopped, the next rule is about leaving. Move on only once the bus signals are off. Even then, keep watching for children and for people with developmental disabilities who may still be near the road. A switched-off light ends the stop, but it does not end your need to look.

lines.text: Across a raised median: slow to ten.
Bus at a school front: pass at ten or less.
Either direction may pass at the school.

narration.text: Two situations replace the full stop with a slow pass. The first is a dual-lane highway with a safety island or raised median. If you are on the other side of that median from a stopped school bus, you slow to ten miles per hour rather than stopping. The second is a school bus stopped directly in front of a school to load or unload. There you may pass it from either direction, but at no more than ten miles per hour. Notice what makes these different from the twenty-five-foot stop: a physical median in the first case, and the school building itself in the second. Both still demand a crawl and watchful eyes.

lines.text: Median rule: slow to ten across the median.
School-front rule: pass at ten or less.
Same speed, different situations.

narration.text: Here is the trap. There are two separate ten miles per hour rules for school buses, and learners often merge them into one. The first is the median rule: on a dual-lane highway, when you are across a safety island or raised median from a stopped school bus, you slow to ten miles per hour. The second is the school-front rule: when the bus is stopped directly in front of a school, you may pass it at no more than ten miles per hour, from either direction. Same speed, different trigger. If a question mentions a median, think highway. If it mentions the school building, think school front.

lines.text: Flashing red lights and a stop arm.
Yield, stop, then pass at fifteen or less.
Across a median: no stop required.

narration.text: Ice cream and frozen dessert trucks follow a rule of their own. When one is showing flashing red lights and a stop signal arm, yield to anyone crossing to or from the truck, stop, and then pass at no more than fifteen miles per hour. Notice the speed is fifteen, not the ten used for school buses. There is also an exception that does not exist in the same form for buses. A driver on the far side of a safety island or raised median on a dual highway does not have to stop for a frozen dessert truck. For a school bus across a median you still slow to ten, but for the dessert truck the stop falls away entirely.

lines.text: Two-lane road, bus flashing red.
How far back, and when to go?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you are on an ordinary two-lane road when a school bus ahead stops and turns on its flashing red lights. How far back must you stop, and when may you move on? Work it out before reading on. You stop at least twenty-five feet away, because a two-lane road calls for the full stop. There is no median to change the rule. Then you stay stopped until the bus signals are off. When they go off, you may move on, but you still watch for children and for people with developmental disabilities who may be crossing. The light going off ends the stop, not the care you owe.

lines.text: Stop for loading buses and flashing reds.
Twenty-five feet, or ten across a median.
Ten at a school front, fifteen for trucks.

narration.text: Let us line the rules up. Stop for a school bus picking up or dropping off children or flashing red lights, and do not rely on its lights, because they could be broken. On a two-lane road, a lines-only highway or a private road, stop at least twenty-five feet away, and go only once the signals are off, still watching for children. Across a raised median on a dual-lane highway, slow to ten. At a school front, pass from either direction at ten or less. For a dessert truck with flashing reds and a stop arm, yield, stop, then pass at fifteen or less, unless a median separates you.

why_how.text: Emergency crews need room to move and to work, so the rules give them a clear lane and a safe distance.
Stopped emergency and service vehicles sit beside moving traffic, and the Move Over law asks drivers to leave them a lane.

scenario.text: Omar sees a tow truck with flashing lights stopped on the right shoulder, and the lane to his left is clear.

reasoning.text: The Move Over law requires moving into a lane not next to the stopped vehicle when safety and traffic allow.

result.text: Omar signals and moves one lane left; had that lane been full, he would slow below the limit and be ready to stop.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking blue lights are not an emergency signal.

correction.text: Volunteer fire and rescue members answering a call use blue lights, and drivers yield to flashing red or blue lights.

memory_support.text: Pull right, stay three hundred back, park two hundred away.

prompt.text: A police car with flashing lights is stopped on the shoulder, but heavy traffic blocks the next lane. What do you do?

answer.text: Slow to a reasonable speed below the posted limit and be ready to stop.

rationale.text: Moving over is the first choice, but when it is unsafe or impossible the law asks you to slow down and be ready to stop.

lines.text: Moving emergency vehicles need a clear path.
Stopped ones need a clear lane.

narration.text: Emergency vehicles create two different situations on the road, and each has its own rule. When an emergency vehicle is moving with its siren or flashing lights, your job is to get out of its way and then keep your distance. When an emergency or service vehicle is stopped at the roadside with its lights flashing, your job is to give it a lane, which is what New Jersey's Move Over law requires. This lesson covers both, along with the colors of emergency lights, the fire hose rule, and the penalties for ignoring the Move Over law. Watch the distances closely, because two of them are easy to swap.

lines.text: Steer to the far right and stop.
Let it pass, then stay three hundred feet back.
Red: police, fire, ambulance. Blue: volunteers.

narration.text: When an emergency vehicle uses its siren or flashing red or blue lights, steer to the far right, stop, and let it pass. After it goes by, stay at least three hundred feet behind any signaling emergency vehicle. Now the colors. Police cars, fire trucks, ambulances and other emergency vehicles use sirens and red lights. Blue lights belong to the private vehicles of volunteer fire and rescue squad members who are answering a call and carry emergency vehicle identification. So a blue light on an ordinary-looking car is still an emergency signal, and the same yielding rule applies to it as to a red light on a fire truck.

lines.text: No parking within two hundred feet.
Never drive over a fire hose.
Unless an official directs you.

narration.text: Fire department vehicles have an extra pair of rules when they are working. Never park within two hundred feet of a fire department vehicle that is in service. Two hundred feet is a long stretch, so look well down the street before you pick a spot. And never drive over a fire hose, unless a fire, rescue or police official tells you to. A hose stretched across the street can look like something you could roll over gently, but the rule is clear: you do not cross it on your own judgment. Only the direction of a fire, rescue or police official changes that, so wait for someone in charge to wave you over.

lines.text: Following distance: at least three hundred feet.
Parking limit: two hundred feet.
Follow three, park two.

narration.text: Here is the pair of numbers that learners most often swap. Two emergency-vehicle distances sit close together in the handbook. The first is a following distance: stay at least three hundred feet behind a signaling emergency vehicle. The second is a parking limit: never park within two hundred feet of a fire department vehicle in service. One is about driving behind a moving vehicle, the other is about where you leave your car near a working fire truck. A simple way to keep them straight is the phrase follow three, park two. Following gets the bigger number, three hundred feet, and parking gets two hundred.

lines.text: Stopped emergency, tow or service vehicle.
Also hazard lights, flares or triangles.
Move to a lane not next to it.

narration.text: The Move Over law covers vehicles that are stopped rather than moving. When you approach a stopped emergency vehicle, tow truck, highway maintenance vehicle or other service vehicle showing flashing lights, or any stopped vehicle using hazard lights, flares or reflective triangles, you must move into a lane that is not next to it, when safety and traffic allow. If moving over is impossible, illegal or unsafe, the fallback is to slow to a reasonable speed below the posted limit and be ready to stop. So there is always something to do: change lanes if you safely can, and slow down if you cannot.

lines.text: Police car stopped on the shoulder.
The next lane is blocked.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a police car with flashing lights is stopped on the right shoulder ahead. You would normally move one lane left, but heavy traffic fills that lane and there is no safe gap. What does the law ask you to do? Work it out before reading on. Moving over is required only when safety and traffic allow, and here they do not. So the fallback applies. Slow to a reasonable speed below the posted limit, and be ready to stop. Forcing your way into the next lane would be unsafe, and keeping your normal speed beside the stopped car would ignore the law entirely.

lines.text: Pull right, stop, then follow three hundred back.
No parking within two hundred feet of a working fire truck.
Move over, or slow down.

narration.text: Let us pull it together. For a siren or flashing red or blue lights, steer to the far right, stop, let the vehicle pass, and stay at least three hundred feet behind it. Red lights mean police, fire or ambulance; blue lights mean volunteer responders in their own cars. Never park within two hundred feet of a fire department vehicle in service, and never drive over a fire hose unless an official tells you to. For a stopped emergency or service vehicle, move into a lane not next to it, or slow below the limit if you cannot. A Move Over violation carries a fine of one hundred to five hundred dollars, and three or more convictions can bring points.

why_how.text: A calm, predictable driver makes a traffic stop go smoothly, which is why the steps focus on staying still and visible.
The roadside is not the place to settle a dispute; there is a later route through court or a complaint.

scenario.text: At night, Priya sees flashing lights behind her, signals and pulls onto the right shoulder.

reasoning.text: She puts the car in park, rolls down the window, turns on the interior light and rests her hands on the wheel.

result.text: Asked for her documents, she says where they are before reaching, then hands over her license, registration and insurance proof.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you should have your documents out before the officer reaches your window.

correction.text: Do not reach for documents, the glove box, the console or under a seat unless told to, and say first what you are about to do.

memory_support.text: Park, window, light, hands, then talk.

prompt.text: An officer has stopped you at night and asks for your registration, which is in the glove box. What do you do?

answer.text: Say that it is in the glove box, and reach for it once told to, with the interior light on and your movements slow.

rationale.text: You keep your hands visible until told otherwise, and you say first what you are about to do before reaching anywhere.

lines.text: Signal, slow, move right.
Then stay calm and visible.

narration.text: Sooner or later most drivers see emergency lights in the mirror. This lesson walks through a police traffic stop from start to finish. First, when emergency lights appear behind you, signal, slow down and move promptly to the right shoulder or another safe place. Then come the steps once you are stopped: what to do with the car, the window, the lights and your hands, which documents to show, how to handle reaching for them, how to respond to instructions, and what to do if you think the stop was unfair. The theme throughout is simple. Be calm, be visible, and be predictable in everything you do.

lines.text: Park, stay inside, roll down the window.
At night, switch on the interior light.
Keep hands visible, ideally on the wheel.
Show license, registration and insurance.

narration.text: Once you have pulled over, put the vehicle in park and stay inside unless the officer tells you otherwise. Roll down the window. At night, switch on the interior light, and keep your hands visible, ideally on the steering wheel. That interior light is one of the few times the handbook wants it on, since interior overhead lights should be used only briefly while driving, or when a police officer asks you to light up the inside of a stopped vehicle. When asked, New Jersey drivers must show a valid driver license, the vehicle registration and proof of insurance. All three are required, not just one.

lines.text: Do not reach unless told to.
Say what you are about to do.
Follow instructions; ask if unclear.
Disagree later, not at the roadside.

narration.text: Here is where well-meaning drivers slip. It feels helpful to dig out your papers before the officer arrives, but the guidance is the opposite. Turn the music down, avoid sudden movements, and do not reach for documents, the glove box, the console or under a seat unless told to, and say first what you are about to do. Follow the officer's instructions, including stepping out of the vehicle if asked, and if an instruction is unclear, politely ask for it to be repeated. If you disagree with the stop, do not argue at the roadside. You can contest the ticket later in court, or file a complaint with the law enforcement agency.

lines.text: Step out if asked.
Ask politely for a repeat.
Court or complaint for disputes.

narration.text: Picture the stop as the officer leading and you following, with a clear path for disagreement afterward. Follow the officer's instructions, including stepping out of the vehicle if you are asked to. If you do not understand an instruction, politely ask for it to be repeated rather than guessing. Guessing can lead to a sudden movement the officer did not expect. And if you believe the stop or the ticket is wrong, the roadside is not where that gets settled. The handbook gives two routes: contest the ticket later in court, or file a complaint with the law enforcement agency involved. Both are open to you after the stop.

lines.text: Stopped at night.
Registration is in the glove box.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: an officer has stopped you at night. Your interior light is on and your hands are on the wheel. The officer asks for your registration, and it is in the glove box. What should you do? Work it out before reading on. Say that the registration is in the glove box before you move, and reach for it only once you are told to. During a police stop you do not reach for documents, the glove box, the console or under a seat unless told to, and you say first what you are about to do. Slow, announced movements keep the stop calm and predictable for everyone.

lines.text: Signal and move to the right shoulder.
Park, window down, light on, hands visible.
Show license, registration, insurance.
Follow instructions; dispute later.

narration.text: Here is the whole traffic stop in order. When emergency lights appear behind you, signal, slow down and move promptly to the right shoulder or another safe place. Put the vehicle in park, stay inside unless told otherwise, roll down the window, switch on the interior light at night and keep your hands visible, ideally on the wheel. Turn the music down and avoid sudden movements. Show a valid license, the registration and proof of insurance, reaching only when told and saying first what you will do. Follow instructions, ask politely for a repeat if unclear, and take any disagreement to court or a complaint later.

why_how.text: Headlights help you see and be seen, so the rules tie them both to the clock and to how far you can see.
High beams that help you can blind other drivers, and glare can cost several seconds of blind driving.

scenario.text: In the middle of a rainy afternoon, Luis switches on his windshield wipers.

reasoning.text: Headlights are required whenever the wipers are in use, and parking lights cannot take their place.

result.text: Luis turns on his headlights, not just his parking lights, even though it is daytime.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking parking lights or fog lights are enough in rain or at dusk.

correction.text: Parking lights or auxiliary lights may not legally take the place of headlights when headlights are required.

memory_support.text: Wipers on, headlights on; high beams only when the road is empty.

prompt.text: It is a foggy morning and visibility is short. You plan to drive with only your fog lights on. Is that enough?

answer.text: No. Headlights are required in fog, and fog lights may only be used together with low beams.

rationale.text: Fog is one of the conditions that requires headlights, and auxiliary lights like fog lights cannot replace them.

lines.text: Headlights: by the clock and by conditions.
Beams and glare affect other drivers.

narration.text: Your vehicle's lights do two jobs. They help you see the road, and they help everyone else see you. But the same lights can also hurt, because a bright beam aimed at another driver can blind them for a moment. This lesson covers when headlights are legally required, both by the time of day and by the conditions around you, why parking lights and fog lights cannot stand in for them, when to use high beams and when to switch to low, what glare does to your eyes and how long it takes to recover, and finally the smaller lights on your car: taillights, dashboard lights, spotlights and hazard flashers.

lines.text: Half an hour after sunset to before sunrise.
Visibility of five hundred feet or less.
Whenever the wipers are in use.
In fog, mist or smoke.

narration.text: Headlights are required by the clock and by conditions. By the clock, they are required from half an hour after sunset until half an hour before sunrise. So dusk counts, even if the sky still looks fairly bright. By conditions, they are also required whenever visibility is five hundred feet or less, whenever the windshield wipers are in use, and in fog, mist, smoke or anything else that cuts visibility. The wiper rule is the easiest to remember and the easiest to forget in daylight: if the wipers are moving, the headlights must be on, even at midday. Either trigger alone is enough to require them.

lines.text: Parking lights cannot replace headlights.
Auxiliary lights cannot replace them either.
Fog lights go with low beams.

narration.text: Here is a common trap. When headlights are required, some drivers switch on only their parking lights, or only their fog lights, and assume that is enough. It is not. Parking lights or auxiliary lights may not legally take the place of headlights when headlights are required. Fog lights are auxiliary lights. They may be used together with low beams to light the road ahead in foggy weather, but they are an addition, not a replacement. So in fog, the low beams go on first, and the fog lights may be added. Driving on fog lights or parking lights alone, when headlights are required, breaks the rule.

lines.text: High beams: open country, no traffic in sight.
Off when a vehicle approaches or you follow.
Low beams: city, traffic, following, meeting.

narration.text: High beams have a narrow use. Use them only in open country with no traffic in sight, and switch them off when another vehicle approaches or when you are following one. Everything else calls for low beams. Low beams are for city driving, heavier traffic, following another vehicle and meeting oncoming vehicles. So the question to ask is simple: is the road ahead empty, and am I in open country? If both answers are yes, high beams are fine. The moment headlights appear ahead, or you come up behind another car, switch back to low beams. Leaving high beams on in those moments puts another driver in your glare.

lines.text: Night pupils are wide open.
Bright beams make them constrict.
Recovery can take three to five seconds.

narration.text: Why does glare matter so much at night? At night the pupils are dilated, opened wide to gather light. Bright beams can blind other drivers for a moment by making their pupils constrict. Recovering from the glare of oncoming high beams can take three to five seconds, and at fifty miles per hour a driver covers the length of a football field in that blind time. So if an oncoming driver has high beams on, look toward the right side of the road until the vehicle passes, rather than staring into the lights. And never flash your own high beams back, however tempting it is to send a signal.

lines.text: Taillights brighten when you brake.
Dashboard dim but readable.
Spotlights and flashers: emergencies only.

narration.text: A few smaller lights round out the picture. Taillights come on with the headlights and parking lights, and they grow brighter when the brakes are applied; in daylight they also light up when you brake. Keep dashboard lights dim enough to avoid glare inside the car, but bright enough to read the dials. Spotlights and hazard flashers are for emergencies only, and spotlights may never be used for driving. That last point catches people out, because a spotlight seems like a way to see farther down a dark road. The rule is firm: a spotlight is never a driving light, and flashers are for emergencies only.

lines.text: Fog cuts visibility.
Fog lights only: enough?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: it is a foggy morning and you can see only a short way ahead. You plan to drive with just your fog lights on, since they are designed for fog. Is that enough? Work it out before reading on. No, it is not. Fog is one of the conditions that requires headlights, along with short visibility and wipers in use. Fog lights are auxiliary lights, and auxiliary lights may not legally take the place of headlights when headlights are required. The right setup is low beams, with fog lights added if you want them, because fog lights may be used together with low beams in foggy weather.

lines.text: Headlights by clock and by conditions.
Never substitute parking or fog lights.
High beams only on empty open roads.
Look right; never flash back.

narration.text: Let us gather the lighting rules. Headlights are required from half an hour after sunset to half an hour before sunrise, and whenever visibility is five hundred feet or less, the wipers are on, or fog, mist or smoke cuts visibility. Parking lights and auxiliary lights cannot replace them, and fog lights go with low beams. Use high beams only in open country with no traffic in sight. Glare can take three to five seconds to recover from, so look toward the right edge and never flash back. Taillights brighten with the brakes, dashboard lights stay dim but readable, and spotlights and flashers are for emergencies.

why_how.text: No-parking distances are measured from specific things, so the skill is matching each distance to its object.
Some places are off limits for stopping or parking altogether, and a breakdown has its own rule: the right shoulder with flashers.

scenario.text: Nia wants to park on a street near a corner with a stop sign and a crosswalk at the intersection.

reasoning.text: She must stay fifty feet from the stop sign and twenty-five feet from the crosswalk, so she checks both distances.

result.text: Nia parks where both distances are met, no more than six inches from the curb.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the fire hydrant distance is the same twenty feet as a fire station driveway.

correction.text: A fire hydrant needs ten feet; twenty feet is for a fire station driveway and the end of a pedestrian safety zone.

memory_support.text: Hydrant ten, crosswalk twenty-five, stop sign fifty.

prompt.text: You want to park near a railroad crossing. How close may you park, and how does that compare with a crosswalk at an intersection?

answer.text: No closer than fifty feet to the crossing; a crosswalk at an intersection needs twenty-five feet.

rationale.text: Railroad crossings share the fifty-foot limit with stop signs, while crosswalks at intersections use twenty-five feet.

lines.text: Distances depend on what is nearby.
Some places are always off limits.

narration.text: Parking rules are mostly about distance. Each rule sets a minimum gap from something specific, such as a fire hydrant, a crosswalk, a stop sign or a fire station. This lesson covers the curb rule, when parked cars need parking lights, each no-parking distance, the two separate twenty-foot rules, the places where you may never stop or park at all, how to open your door safely, and what to do when your car breaks down. Several of these distances are close together, so we will learn them one by one and then put them side by side, which is where most mistakes happen.

lines.text: No more than six inches from the curb.
Parking lights outside business or residential zones.

narration.text: Start at the curb. Parking a vehicle more than six inches from the curb is illegal, so pull in close. A car left a foot away is breaking the rule. Next, lighting. Parking lights are required on vehicles parked anywhere other than business or residential zones. In other words, the requirement applies outside those two kinds of zones, and a car parked there must show parking lights. Keep this separate from the headlight rule you learned earlier: while you are driving, parking lights may never replace headlights, but while you are parked outside those zones, parking lights are required.

lines.text: Fire hydrant: ten feet.
Crosswalk at an intersection: twenty-five feet.
Railroad crossing or stop sign: fifty feet.

narration.text: Now the core distances. Do not park within ten feet of a fire hydrant. Do not park within twenty-five feet of a crosswalk at an intersection, except at alleys. And do not park within fifty feet of a railroad crossing, or within fifty feet of a stop sign. Notice that the railroad crossing and the stop sign share the same number. That pairing is worth remembering as a unit: rails and stop signs, fifty feet. The hydrant is the smallest distance, ten feet, and the crosswalk sits in the middle at twenty-five. Saying them in order, ten, twenty-five, fifty, helps them stick as a single ladder from small to large.

lines.text: Fire station driveway: twenty feet.
Across the street from the entrance: seventy-five feet.
Safety zone end: also twenty feet.

narration.text: Fire stations get two distances. Do not park within twenty feet of a fire station driveway on the same side of the street, or within seventy-five feet of the entrance when you are on the opposite side of the street. The larger number across the street can seem backward, so learn it as its own rule: near side twenty, far side seventy-five. There is also a second twenty-foot rule that has nothing to do with fire stations. Do not park within twenty feet of the end of a pedestrian safety zone. So twenty feet appears twice: once for the fire station driveway, and once for the end of a pedestrian safety zone.

lines.text: Hydrant ten, not twenty.
Crosswalk twenty-five, not twenty.
Stop sign fifty, like rails.

narration.text: Here is the trap. These parking distances are easy to blur because several of them are near each other. The fire hydrant is ten feet, and learners often push it up to twenty because it feels related to the fire station. The fire station driveway is twenty, and so is the end of a pedestrian safety zone. The crosswalk at an intersection is twenty-five, which is easy to round down to twenty. The railroad crossing and the stop sign are both fifty. And across the street from a fire station entrance, it is seventy-five. When a question names an object, match the object first, and the number will follow.

lines.text: Crosswalks, sidewalks, bus stops, driveways.
Intersections, interstates, bridges, tunnels.
Beside a car parked at the curb.
Disability spaces without authorization.

narration.text: Some places are off limits no matter how far you are from a hydrant or a sign. Never stop or park in a crosswalk, on a sidewalk, in a bus stop zone, in front of a driveway, inside an intersection, on an interstate, on a bridge, an elevated roadway or in a tunnel, next to a car already parked at the curb, or in a disability space without authorization. There is one situation where stopping at the roadside is expected. If your vehicle has mechanical trouble or another emergency, stop on the right shoulder and turn on the emergency flashers. That is a breakdown stop, not a parking spot, and the flashers tell other drivers why you are there.

lines.text: Parking near a railroad crossing.
Compare with a crosswalk.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you want to park on a street that runs near a railroad crossing, and there is also a crosswalk at the next intersection. How close may you park to the crossing, and how does that compare with the crosswalk? Work it out before reading on. You may park no closer than fifty feet to the railroad crossing. That is the same distance as a stop sign. The crosswalk at the intersection needs twenty-five feet, which is half as far. So you need to check two separate distances here, fifty feet from the rails and twenty-five feet from the crosswalk, and park only where both are met.

lines.text: Within six inches of the curb.
Ten, twenty, twenty-five, fifty, seventy-five.
Check for bikes before opening the door.

narration.text: Here is the parking lesson in one view. Park no more than six inches from the curb, and show parking lights outside business or residential zones. Keep ten feet from a hydrant, twenty-five from a crosswalk at an intersection, fifty from a railroad crossing or stop sign, twenty from a fire station driveway or a safety zone end, and seventy-five across from a fire station entrance. Never park in a tunnel, on a bridge, beside a parked car, or in the other banned places. Before opening the driver-side door, check for traffic and hard-to-see bicycles and mopeds, because a driver who opens a door into traffic may be liable; passengers should exit on the curb side.

why_how.text: Handheld phone use while driving is a primary offense, and the fines rise with each repeat offense.
New drivers and school bus drivers carry tighter limits, with GDL holders barred from even hands-free phones.

scenario.text: Eli, a GDL holder, wants to take a call through his car's hands-free system while driving.

reasoning.text: Hands-free is legal for ordinary drivers, but a GDL holder may not use a handheld or hands-free phone while driving.

result.text: Eli lets the call go and returns it once he is no longer driving.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a hands-free phone is legal for every driver.

correction.text: Hands-free is legal but strongly discouraged for ordinary drivers; GDL holders, and school bus drivers driving the bus, may not use one.

memory_support.text: Handheld banned, hands-free discouraged, GDL none.

prompt.text: A school bus driver, parked in a safe place off the highway, needs to make a hands-free call. Is it allowed?

answer.text: Yes. A school bus driver may use a phone when parked in a safe place off the highway, or in an emergency.

rationale.text: The ban covers driving the bus; parking safely off the highway is one of the two exceptions.

lines.text: Handheld phones are a primary offense.
Some drivers face stricter rules.

narration.text: This lesson covers phones and other devices behind the wheel, and finishes with littering. Using a handheld phone or texting device while driving on any public road in New Jersey is a primary offense, which means it is a violation in its own right. A hands-free phone is legal for most drivers, but strongly discouraged. From there, we look at the narrow emergency exception and how a driver might prove it, the fines and points for repeat offenses, the stricter rules for GDL holders and school bus drivers, a law that treats illegal phone use as recklessness, and the rules on trash thrown from or carried in a vehicle.

lines.text: Handheld or texting: primary offense.
Hands-free: legal but strongly discouraged.
Emergency only, one hand on the wheel.

narration.text: The basic rule draws a line between handheld and hands-free. Using a handheld phone or texting device while driving on any public road is a primary offense. A hands-free phone is legal, but strongly discouraged. There is one exception to the handheld ban. A handheld phone may be used only in an emergency, such as a fire, a traffic crash, a serious road hazard, a medical emergency or a hazardous material emergency, and even then one hand must stay on the wheel. So the exception is narrow and specific. A routine call, a quick text at a red light or checking a message in slow traffic does not qualify.

lines.text: Emergency proof: testimony, statements, phone records.
Fines rise with each offense.
Third or later: three points, possible suspension.

narration.text: If you do use a handheld phone in an emergency, you may need to show it. To prove the use was legal, a driver may have to provide testimony or written statements from the authorities, or phone records. Now the penalties for illegal use. Handheld phone fines are two hundred to four hundred dollars for a first offense, four hundred to six hundred dollars for a second within ten years, and six hundred to eight hundred dollars for a third or later offense. A third or later offense also brings three points, and possibly a ninety-day suspension. The cost climbs steeply with each repeat offense.

lines.text: GDL holders: no handheld or hands-free.
No other handheld electronic devices.
School bus drivers: none while driving the bus.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Because hands-free phones are legal for ordinary drivers, many people assume they are legal for everyone. They are not. A GDL holder may not use a handheld or hands-free phone, or any other handheld electronic device, while driving. A school bus driver may not use a handheld or hands-free phone while driving the bus, except in an emergency or when parked in a safe place off the highway. So there are three levels. Ordinary drivers: handheld banned, hands-free allowed. GDL holders: no phone at all while driving. School bus drivers: no phone while driving the bus, with two narrow exceptions.

lines.text: Kulesh's, Kuberts' and Bolis' Law.
Enacted in two thousand twelve.
Illegal phone use counts as recklessness.

narration.text: Phone use can also carry consequences far beyond a fine. Kulesh's, Kuberts' and Bolis' Law, enacted in two thousand twelve, treats illegal cell phone use while driving as recklessness under the vehicular homicide and assault by auto statutes. In plain terms, if illegal phone use is part of a crash covered by those statutes, the law treats that phone use as reckless driving behavior. This is why the handheld ban is not a minor rule. A choice that seems small, like glancing at a message, can be treated as recklessness under some of the most serious driving laws there are. Keep the phone away unless the law allows it.

lines.text: Throwing trash from a vehicle is illegal.
Dangerous objects: fines up to one thousand dollars.
Cover any trash or debris you carry.

narration.text: The last rules are about what leaves your vehicle. Throwing trash from a moving or parked vehicle is illegal. Throwing dangerous objects onto a roadway can bring fines of up to one thousand dollars, and littering from a moving vehicle can cost the driver the license. So the penalty can reach the license itself, not just the wallet. There is also a rule about what you carry. Any trash, debris or rubbish carried in a vehicle must be covered so it cannot litter the road. So a pickup full of loose yard waste or old boxes needs a cover before it leaves the driveway.

lines.text: School bus parked safely off the highway.
Hands-free call: allowed?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a school bus driver has pulled the bus into a safe place off the highway and parked it. The driver needs to make a hands-free call. Is that allowed? Work it out before reading on. Yes, it is. A school bus driver may not use a handheld or hands-free phone while driving the bus, but the rule has two exceptions: an emergency, and being parked in a safe place off the highway. This driver is parked safely off the highway, so the call is allowed. Compare a GDL holder, who may not use any phone while driving, and an ordinary driver, for whom hands-free is legal but discouraged.

lines.text: Handheld: primary offense, emergency only.
GDL holders and bus drivers: stricter.
Illegal use can count as recklessness.
Never throw trash; cover your load.

narration.text: Let us pull it together. Handheld phone use while driving is a primary offense, and hands-free is legal but strongly discouraged. A handheld phone may be used only in an emergency, with one hand on the wheel, and proving it may take testimony, statements or phone records. Fines rise with each offense, and a third or later offense adds three points and possibly a suspension. GDL holders may not use any phone while driving, and school bus drivers may not while driving the bus. Illegal phone use can count as recklessness under serious crash laws. Never throw trash from a vehicle, and keep any trash you carry covered.
